{"id": "f212795d-124d-47f5-beea-6b70e8523d4c", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_mmmzKWG6C1mSDnJ8XHuqP4", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html\",\"content\":\"# How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock\\n\\nWhen you run model inference, there are quotas on the number of tokens that can be processed depending on which Amazon Bedrock model you use. Review the following terminology related to token quotas:\\n\\n| Term | Definition |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| `InputTokenCount` | The CloudWatch Amazon Bedrock runtime metric that represents the number of input tokens processed by the model, excluding cached tokens. To determine your total input token consumption against your quota, sum `InputTokenCount + CacheWriteInputTokenCount`. |\\n| `OutputTokenCount` | The CloudWatch Amazon Bedrock runtime metric that represents the number of tokens generated by the model in response to a request. |\\n| `CacheReadInputTokenCount` | The CloudWatch Amazon Bedrock runtime metric that represents the number of input tokens that were successfully retrieved from a cache instead of being reprocessed by the model. This value is 0 if you don't use prompt caching. |\\n| `CacheWriteInputTokenCount` | The CloudWatch Amazon Bedrock runtime metric that represents the number of input tokens that were successfully written into the cache. This value is 0 if you don't use prompt caching. |\\n| Tokens per minute (TPM) | A quota set by AWS at the model level on the number of tokens (including both input and output) that you can use in one minute. |\\n| Tokens per day (TPD) | Maximum tokens per day across all supported Amazon Bedrock models for this account. Token count is estimated based on on-demand pricing; actual token consumption varies by model, input/output ratio, and cache usage. |\\n| `max_tokens` | A parameter you provide in your request to set a maximum amount of output tokens the model can generate. |\\n| Burndown rate | The rate at which input and output tokens are converted into token quota usage for the throttling system. |\\n\\nThe burndown rate for Anthropic Claude models version 4.8 is **15x for output tokens** (1 output token consumes 15 tokens from your quotas) and the burndown rate for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Fable 5.2 is **10x for output tokens**. The burndown rate for Anthropic Claude Mythos 5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and Claude Mythos 5.2 is **2.5x for output tokens** (1 output token consumes 2.5 tokens from your quotas). For Anthropic Claude Fable 5 and all other Anthropic models version 4.7 and below, the burndown is **5x for output tokens** (1 output token consumes 5 tokens from your quotas).\\n\\nThe burndown rate for OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, and GPT-5.6 Luna on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint is **10x for output tokens** (1 output token consumes 10 tokens from your quotas).\\n\\nUnless otherwise specified in the model card, the burndown rate for all other models is **1:1** (1 output token consumes 1 token from your quota).\\n\\nToken burndown rates apply only to models available on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. Models available exclusively on the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint have separate quotas for input and output tokens, so burndown does not apply.\\n\\n###### Topics\\n\\n* Understanding token quota management\\n* Understanding the impact of the max_tokens parameter\\n* Optimizing the max_tokens parameter\\n\\n## Understanding token quota management\\n\\nWhen you make a request, tokens are deducted from your TPM and TPD quotas.\\nCalculations occur at the following stages:\\n\\n* **At the start of the request** \u2013 The\\n  following sum is deducted from your quotas. The request is throttled if you\\n  exceed a quota.\\n\\n  ```\\n  Total input tokens + max_tokens\\n  ```\\n* **During processing** \u2013 The quota\\n  consumed by the request is periodically adjusted to account for the actual\\n  number of output tokens generated.\\n* **At the end of the request** \u2013 The\\n  total number of tokens consumed by the request will be calculated as follows and any unused tokens are replenished to your quota:\\n\\n  ```\\n  InputTokenCount + CacheWriteInputTokenCount + (OutputTokenCount x burndown rate)\\n  ```\\n\\n  `CacheReadInputTokenCount` don't contribute to this calculation and are not counted toward your quota. If you don't use prompt caching, both `CacheWriteInputTokenCount` and `CacheReadInputTokenCount` will be 0.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nYou're only billed for your actual token usage.\\n\\nFor example, if you use Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4 and send a request containing 1,000 input tokens and it generates a response equivalent to 100 tokens:\\n\\n* **1,500 tokens** (1,000 + 100 x 5) will be depleted from your TPM and TPD quotas.\\n* You'll only be billed for **1,100 tokens**.\\n\\n## Understanding the impact of the max_tokens parameter\\n\\nThe `max_tokens` value is deducted from your quota at the beginning of each request. If you\u2019re hitting TPM quotas earlier than expected, try reducing `max_tokens` to better approximate the size of your completions.\\n\\nThe following scenarios provide examples of how quota deductions would have worked on completed requests using a model that has a 5x burndown rate for output tokens::\\n\\n### Scenario 1: High max_tokens value\\n\\nAssume the following parameters:\\n\\n* **InputTokenCount:** 3,000\\n* **CacheReadInputTokenCount:** 4,000\\n* **CacheWriteInputTokenCount:** 1,000\\n* **OutputTokenCount:** 1,000\\n* **max_tokens:** 32,000\\n\\nThe following quota deductions take place:\\n\\n* **Initial deduction when request is made:** 36,000 (= 3,000 + 1,000 + 32,000)\\n* **Final adjusted deduction after response is generated:** 9,000 (= 3,000 + 1,000 + 1,000 x 5)\\n\\nIn this scenario, fewer concurrent requests could be made because the `max_tokens` parameter was set too high. This reduces the request concurrency, throughput, and quota use, because the TPM quota capacity would be reached quickly.\\n\\n### Scenario 2: Optimized max_tokens value\\n\\nAssume the following parameters:\\n\\n* **InputTokenCount:** 3,000\\n* **CacheReadInputTokenCount:** 4,000\\n* **CacheWriteInputTokenCount:** 1,000\\n* **OutputTokenCount:** 1,000\\n* **max_tokens:** 1,250\\n\\nThe following quota deductions take place:\\n\\n* **Initial deduction when request is made:** 5,250 (= 3,000 + 1,000 + 1,250)\\n* **Final adjusted deduction after response is generated:** 9,000 (= 3,000 + 1,000 + 1,000 x 5)\\n\\nIn this scenario, the `max_tokens` parameter was optimized, because the initial deduction is only slightly higher than the final adjusted deduction. This helped increase the request concurrency, throughput, and quota use.\\n\\n## Optimizing the max_tokens parameter\\n\\nBy optimizing the `max_tokens` parameter, you can efficiently use your allocated quota capacity. To help inform your decision about this parameter, you can use Amazon CloudWatch, which automatically collects metrics from AWS services, including token usage data in Amazon Bedrock.\\n\\nTokens are recorded in the `InputTokenCount` and `OutputTokenCount` runtime metrics (for more metrics, see Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics.\\n\\nTo use CloudWatch monitoring to inform your decision of the `max_tokens` parameter, do the following in the AWS Management Console:\\n\\n1. Sign in to the Amazon CloudWatch console at <https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch>.\\n2. From the left navigation pane, select **Dashboards**.\\n3. Select the **Automatic dashboards** tab.\\n4. Select **Bedrock**.\\n5. In the **Token Counts by Model** dashboard, select the expand icon.\\n6. Select a time duration and range parameters for the metrics to account for\\n   peak usage.\\n7. From the dropdown menu labeled **Sum**, you can choose\\n   different metrics to observe your token usage. Examine these metrics to\\n   guide your decision on setting your `max_tokens` value.\",\"total_length\":7507,\"start_index\":0,\"end_index\":7507,\"truncated\":false,\"redirected_url\":null,\"error_code\":null}]}}"}]}], "label": "Read Bedrock token quota burndown documentation"}

{"id": "0ecf75ba-18ae-4567-849f-74c0072b056d", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_sZQUppwSYmyTZMrkgaVOfj", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-throttling-error\",\"content\":\"# How do I troubleshoot the \\\"ThrottlingException\\\" error when I use Amazon Bedrock on-demand resources?\\n\\nI want to troubleshoot the \\\"ThrottlingException\\\" 429 HTTP status code error that I receive when I use Amazon Bedrock on-demand resources.\\n\\n---\\n\\nShort description\\n-----------------\\n\\nWhen you exceed service quotas, Amazon Bedrock denies your requests.\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock returns a \\\"ThrottlingException\\\" HTTP Status Code: 429 error, and you receive one of the following error messages on the client side:\\n\\n*   \\\"Too many requests, please wait before trying again. You have sent too many requests. Wait before trying again.\\\"\\n*   \\\"Your request rate is too high. Reduce the frequency of requests.\\\"\\n*   \\\"Too many tokens, please wait before trying again.\\\"\\n*   \\\"Too many tokens per day, please wait before trying again.\\\"\u00a0\\n\\nResolution\\n----------\\n\\n**Note:** If you receive errors when you run AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) commands, then see [Troubleshooting errors for the AWS CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-chap-troubleshooting.html). Also, make sure that [you're using the most recent AWS CLI version](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html).\\n\\n### Monitor your AWS service quotas\\n\\nReview your [Amazon Bedrock service quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas.html) to make sure that you didn't exceed them. Check Amazon CloudWatch metrics at 1-minute increments to identify throttling patterns. When your usage exceeds the quotas at peak times, resource throttle can occur even with previously successful batches. To make sure that your application's request volume doesn't exceed the quotas, monitor the\u00a0**InputTokenCount** and **Invocations** [Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-runtime-metrics.html).\\n\\nSpecific models have separate quotas for Requests Per Minute (RPM) and Tokens Per Minute (TPM) that Amazon Bedrock enforces concurrently.\\n\\nNewer model versions can have different quotas than previous versions.\\n\\n**Note:** The Service Quota dashboard shows only configured quotas, not real-time usage. To monitor real-time usage, use CloudWatch.\\n\\n### Use cross-Region inference profiles\\n\\n[Use Cross-Region inference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles-use.html) for workloads that process outside a single AWS Region. Use geographic cross-Region inference to make sure that data processing stays within specific geographic boundaries. Choose Global cross-Region inference for cost savings without geographic restrictions.\\n\\nSpecific foundational models require cross-Region inference profiles in specific Regions. Specific foundational models also offer global inference profiles that route requests to supported commercial AWS Regions worldwide.\\n\\nFor more information, see the code sample for cross-Region inference in the [amazon-bedrock-workshop](https://github.com/aws-samples/amazon-bedrock-workshop) on the GitHub website.\\n\\n**Note:** To use an inference profile, you must\u00a0use a [AWS Region and model that Amazon Bedrock supports](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles-support.html).\\n\\n### Request a quota increase\\n\\nNew AWS accounts might have lower initial quotas than the default quotas. Specific models have non-adjustable fixed quotas. If your workload traffic exceeds your account's on-demand quotas, then contact [AWS Support](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awssupport/latest/user/case-management.html#creating-a-support-case) or your account manager to [request a quota increase](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-increase.html). AWS might adjust default quotas based on usage patterns or service requirements.\\n\\nInclude the following information in your request:\\n\\n*   The name of the quota to increase\\n*   Your current quota value and the quota value that you require\\n*   The model ID\\n*   The Region for the quota increase\\n*   A brief explanation of your use case\\n*   Your projected usage, including steady and peak tokens and requests per minute, and average input and output tokens per request\\n\\n### Use Provisioned Throughput\\n\\nIf you have high throughput requirements, then purchase Provisioned Throughput.\\n\\n**Note:** When you use Provisioned Throughput, you incur charges. For information, see [Amazon Bedrock pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/#bedrock-pricing-models).\\n\\nFor more information about Provisioned Throughput, see [Use a Provisioned Throughput with an Amazon Bedrock resource](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-thru-use.html). To use the AWS CLI or Python SDK to create Provisioned Throughput, see [Code examples for Provisioned Throughput](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-thru-code-samples.html).\\n\\n**Note:** Before you purchase Provisioned Throughput, make sure that you use a [Region and model that Amazon Bedrock supports](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-thru-supported.html).\\n\\n### Add retries with exponential backoff\\n\\nWhen you use on-demand mode, Amazon Bedrock uses a shared capacity pool across multiple customers. High service demand can throttle your resources even when your requests stay within your account's quotas. Also, the service automatically manages capacity allocation across all users.\\n\\nIt's best practice to use retries with [exponential backoff and jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/). If you use AWS SDKs, then see [Retry behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/feature-retry-behavior.html).\\n\\nMake sure that the retry backoff lasts 1 full minute when it reaches per-minute quotas. Sync your retry attempts with the 60-second quota refresh cycle. Also, distribute your requests across multiple seconds within a 1-minute period.\\n\\nExample Python configuration with adaptive retry mode:\\n\\n```plaintext\\nfrom botocore.config import Config\\n\\nconfig = Config(\\n    retries={\\n        'max_attempts': 10,  # Default is 3\\n        'mode': 'adaptive'\\n    }\\n)\\nbedrock_runtime = boto3.client('bedrock-runtime', config=config)\\n```\\n\\n### Resolve the \\\"ServiceUnavailable\\\" error\\n\\nA \\\"ServiceUnavailable\\\" error occurs because of temporary capacity constraints, not exceeded quotas. This error usually automatically resolves, but can require architecture adjustments for critical workloads.\\n\\nReview your AWS CloudTrail logs to check whether you receive a \\\"ServiceUnavailable\\\" error with the \\\"ThrottlingException\\\" error.\\n\\nIf you receive both errors, then take the following actions to resolve the \\\"ServiceUnavailable\\\" error:\\n\\n*   Check the [AWS Health Dashboard](https://health.aws.amazon.com/health/status) for service disruptions.\\n*   [Implement retries](https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter.pdf?did=ba_card-body&trk=ba_card-body) with exponential backoff and jitter.\\n*   [Use CloudWatch Logs to monitor](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html) the \\\"ServiceUnavailable\\\" error separately from the \\\"ThrottlingException\\\" error.\\n*   [Use cross-Region inference profiles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cross-region-inference.html) to distribute traffic to other Regions when one Region is unavailable.\\n\\n### Resolve unexpected throttle when you didn't exceed quotas\\n\\nIf you experienced throttle and you didn't exceed service quotas, then take the following actions:\\n\\n*   [Check the Regional service health](https://health.aws.amazon.com/health/status).\\n*   [Contact Support](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awssupport/latest/user/case-management.html#creating-a-support-case) to troubleshoot account-specific configurations.\",\"total_length\":7759,\"start_index\":0,\"end_index\":7759,\"truncated\":false,\"redirected_url\":null,\"error_code\":null}]}}"}]}], "label": "Read Bedrock throttling troubleshooting article"}

{"id": "810caca0-bf51-47bc-aea8-5b1fd0b170de", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Bedrock enforces more than a requests-per-minute (RPM) limit. For most models it also enforces a tokens-per-minute (TPM) quota, and often a tokens-per-day (TPD) quota, at the same time. If you exceed any one of them, you get a throttling error (HTTP 429), even when RPM is well under its limit.

**Common causes**

1. **TPM is the limit you're hitting, not RPM.** Input and output tokens both count toward TPM. A few large requests can use up TPM while RPM stays low.

2. **Output tokens count for more than one token each.** This is called the burndown rate. For Anthropic Claude models:
   - Output tokens count 5x for version 4.7 and below, and for Fable 5.
   - They count 10x for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Fable 5.1 and Fable 5.2.
   - They count 15x for version 4.8.
   - They count 2.5x for the Mythos 5 family.
   - OpenAI GPT-5.6 models count 10x.

   Most other models count 1:1. You're billed only for the tokens actually used, but the quota is charged at the burndown rate.

3. **`max_tokens` is reserved up front.** At the start of each request, Bedrock deducts `input tokens + max_tokens` from your quota. When the request finishes, it refunds the unused part. If `max_tokens` is set to 32,000 and the real response is 1,000 tokens, each in-flight request holds a large reservation. A burst of concurrent requests can hit TPM quickly, and this is a very common cause. The fix is to set `max_tokens` close to your realistic response size.

4. **Per-minute quotas are hit in short bursts.** If requests cluster in a few seconds, you can hit the limit even when the per-minute average looks fine. CloudWatch at 1-minute resolution can hide this.

5. **Prompt caching affects the count.** Cache writes count toward your quota. Cache reads don't.

6. **The daily token quota (TPD) can also throttle you.** The error message "Too many tokens per day" tells you this is the cause.

7. **On-demand capacity is shared.** Bedrock's docs say high demand across customers can throttle you even when you're within your quotas. This usually shows up as `ServiceUnavailable` alongside `ThrottlingException`. Check the AWS Health Dashboard for the Region. If you still see throttling with no quota exceeded and no health issue, contact Support so they can check your account-specific configuration.

8. **Quotas differ by model and Region.** Newer model versions can have lower quotas than older ones. New accounts also often start with lower quotas.

**How to confirm which one it is**
- Read the error text. "Too many requests" points to RPM. "Too many tokens" points to TPM. "Too many tokens per day" points to TPD.
- In CloudWatch, compare `InputTokenCount`, `CacheWriteInputTokenCount` and `OutputTokenCount` (the output × burndown rate) against your TPM quota. Also check `Invocations`, and look at 1-minute granularity.
- Compare your `max_tokens` setting with your actual average output length.

**Fixes**
- Lower `max_tokens` to match real output sizes.
- Add retries with exponential backoff and jitter. Use boto3 `adaptive` mode, and let backoff last up to a full minute when you hit a per-minute limit.
- Spread requests out over the minute instead of sending them in bursts.
- Use cross-Region inference profiles (geographic or global) to draw on more capacity.
- Request a quota increase. Include the model ID, Region, and your steady and peak tokens per minute.
- For sustained, predictable load, consider Provisioned Throughput or Reserved Tier where the model supports it.

I can check your account's actual `Invocations`, `InputTokenCount` and `OutputTokenCount` metrics and throttle counts for a specific model and Region. Tell me which model ID, Region and time window to use.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
